title: Halcyon Expanse
dialogue: NAME on its own line. (action) smaller. Quoted speech italic.

chapter.title: Arrival
chapter.note: Re-chunked denser slides (~40–80 words/page). Engagement deferred. Shuttle trio wired.

pages.band: The ship is quiet in the way a ship is quiet when the work has already started without you. Behind the glass Halden-4 fills the frame, amber and slow, a world with weather and a clock. Eli Hale stands with his hands in his jacket and lets the planet do the talking.

He has been aboard eleven hours. He knows the sound of a relief hull. He does not know this one yet. The Vesper is small on purpose. People live close. Coffee lives longer than it should. Someone has already written his name on a board in a room he has not seen.

Even up here the vents bring a dry chalk smell when the planet wind turns — the kind that lives in old classrooms.

The letter that brought him was one page. A clinic on Halden-4 is supposed to open tonight. The ground people have been waiting on doors. The ship needed a systems engineer who would look at the site and say what was true. That was the whole invitation. No romance in it. No warning.

Halden-4 is not empty. It is thin. A few roofs. A pad. A clinic meant to take breath and give it back by evening. Official language calls that occupancy. People on the ground call it the first night they are allowed to walk in.

The last place he stood left a mark that does not show on a face. A room that wanted a kind number. He said the other number anyway. He is not proud of how it ended. He is not ashamed. Work is work. You look. You say what is true. You live with the room after.

That is why the ticket made sense. Not a new family. A clock, and a ship that needed someone who would not decorate a paragraph. He turns. The corridor will smell like metal and other people’s mornings.

He is thirty-four. He reads rooms the way some men read faces. Power. Air. The talk between machines. The small lie a file tells when it has been copied too many times. He is not command. He is not a lieutenant. He is the person you want when two clocks disagree and both of them are polite.

The jacket is still too clean for this ship. That will last a day. Inside the left pocket a short patch lead waits — not Vesper issue, worn soft at the grips. He used it the last time a room wanted a kind number. He said the other number. The lead came with him.

He came up through yards and grids and relief hulls that all smelled a little like this one. He is good at the quiet work. He is less good at being new. He puts his hands in his pockets because the alternative is touching a bulkhead he does not own yet.

Somewhere ahead a woman is already tired of waiting on a second voice. He goes to find her.

She finds him before the welcome does. She has the walk of someone who has already done three jobs before breakfast. She does not offer a tour. She offers a direction.

REYES (without slowing)
"You're Hale. Maddox wants you first. Holm filed a welcome. It is still a file. We have a clinic on the clock."

He matches her pace. The corridor is narrow enough that you learn a person by how they do not run you into a bulkhead. Reyes does not. That is a kind of kindness. It is also a kind of hurry. She has been on Vesper long enough that the ship has a shape in her shoulders.

REYES (over her shoulder, almost a smile)
"Don't rehearse on the way. She can smell a speech from the hatch. She wants a voice that is not the slate."

Eli nods. It is the first useful thing he has done since the gallery.

They pass the mess because every path on Vesper passes the mess. Two mugs. A lamp that has outlived three captains. The planet in the window like a fact no one has to vote on. When the vents cycle, the chalk smell comes again — faint, stubborn, like a blackboard no one has washed.

This is how a small ship tells you the truth. Not in a briefing. In the way cups are left for the next watch. In the notes stuck to a bulkhead in two handwritings. In the quiet that is not empty, only busy somewhere else.

Reyes does not stop. She tips her chin at the window as if Eli might have missed the world.

REYES
"Clinic is that way when we go down. Tonight if the paper holds. People on the ground have been sleeping in a school. If you hear chalk in the air, that is them waiting."

pages.top: The door with the light under it.
pages.band: The briefing hatch leaks map-light onto the deck. Someone inside is already talking in the low voice people use when a clock is in the room. A folded sheet waits in the door rack where welcomes go when the person who wrote them does not walk them in.

Eli puts his hand on the frame and does not go in until Reyes does. That is not fear. That is manners. You do not own a threshold you have not been given.

He can smell cold coffee. He can hear a name that is not his. Then Reyes knocks once with her knuckle, which is not a request.

REYES
"Hale."

The talking stops. The door knows how to open.

pages.top: The room is too small for the map.
pages.band:
The table is older than the ship’s paint. A map is pinned as if paper still matters. Four people can stand here if no one breathes like they own the place. Coffee has gone cold in a cup with no name on it. Holm’s welcome still sits folded at the corner, unopened.

Maddox does not look up at once. That is not rudeness. That is a woman finishing a sentence in her head. When she does look, it is the look you give a tool you have not tested.

The map has a square in pencil. Clinic. Open tonight. Around the square, smaller marks that mean power, air, talk between the prefab and the ship. Her thumb finds the school mark outside the square and stays there half a breath too long — long enough to mean she has already done the math for the people sleeping on those floors. Then the thumb moves. Eli does not speak yet. Rooms like this punish the first sentence if it is decoration.

MADDOX (still on the map)
"Holm wanted a welcome. I wanted a second pair of eyes before we tell the ground they can walk in. Sit if you want. I wouldn't."

He does not sit. Reyes takes the wall and becomes furniture in the useful way.

Maddox turns a slate so he can see it. The official story is short. The clinic is clean. The power is steady. The doors may open this evening. The colonial clock is printed as if clocks were stone.

Someone needed that paragraph to be true. That is not the same thing as it being true.

On the borrowed board at Eli’s elbow the clinic is not a paragraph. It is a live thing talking to Vesper. Every nine minutes the power stutters. Short. Ugly. Then it pretends it did not. The slate cannot see that. The slate was written by people who needed tonight more than they needed a second instrument.

Paper says ready. The ship says hitching. If they open on the clock, someone on the ground inherits that hitch in the dark — chalk in the vents and all.

MADDOX
"The slate says we open tonight. I asked for you because I am tired of being the only person in the room who does not love a paragraph. What do you see."

The room waits. Not as a game. As a room.

Eli puts two fingers on the board where the stutter lives and lets the room watch the next nine minutes arrive on schedule.

ELI
"The slate is kind. The board is not. Prefab power hitching every nine minutes. Short. Ugly. Then it pretends. If we open on the colonial clock, the people in that school inherit the hitch in the dark."

The room changes temperature without anyone touching the air. Maddox’s thumb leaves the school mark as if the decision took the heat with it.

MADDOX
"Then tonight waits until the power makes sense. Warm the shuttle. Hale comes. We look at the thing that is lying."

Reyes is already off the wall.

REYES
"About time somebody said the quiet part with the board still glowing."

They leave Holm’s welcome folded where it was. The corridor takes them past the mess without stopping. The chalk smell rides the vents harder as the shuttle bay opens its throat — craft waiting, Halden-4 bright beyond the door.

Eli’s hand finds the patch lead in his pocket and lets it go. Habits do not fix a prefab. Eyes do.

Reyes straps in like someone who has done this drop before breakfast. Eli finds the rail. Maddox does not smile. She does not need to.

REYES (strapping in)
"If the paper was going to hold, we would already be late for a party. Hold the rail. Dust has opinions."

The shuttle drops toward a pad that has been waiting on doors. Through the bay frame the prefab is still only a hint — a box and heat and the promise of chalk. The colonial clock does not care how the drop feels.
It is smaller than the map promised and quieter than the slate allowed. Heat comes off the pad. The chalk smell is stronger here, mixed with dust that has been waiting on doors.

pages.top: Nine minutes is not a theory.
pages.band:
You can feel the hitch if you stand still with your hand on the rail — short, ugly, then the quiet that pretends it did not happen.

People on the ground will sleep under this roof tonight if the clock wins. From here the school is a low shape and a rumor of beds. The clinic is a box that talks and then does not.

Maddox walks the perimeter like a woman counting lies. Reyes watches the sky for the ship’s shadow and finds it. Eli watches the rail through another nine minutes because once is a story and twice is a system.

MADDOX
"We do not open what we have not watched fail. Holm can keep his welcome folded until we have something true to walk into."

REYES (quiet)
"School’s still full. Clock’s still a clock. At least the paragraph stopped winning by itself."

The shuttle ticks as it cools. The clinic is still on the board. The next hour belongs to whoever is honest first.

Chapter one ends here.
